title: Advancing Molecule Invariant Representation via Privileged Substructure Identification

problem.claim: Molecule representation models struggle with out-of-distribution changes in molecule size or scaffold when properties remain identical.

gap.claim: Existing molecule invariant learning needs to incorporate invariant privileged substructures and use environment splits compatible with molecule invariant learning.

contributions.claim: MILI formalizes molecule invariant learning around privileged substructure identification and introduces a substructure invariance constraint.
The framework establishes two criteria for environment splits that support molecule invariant learning.
MILI uses a dual-head graph neural network whose shared identifier identifies privileged substructures and whose environment and task heads predict from variant and privileged substructures.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe MILI as a novel framework.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that MILI's molecule invariant learning and environment split mutually enhance each other according to their theoretical analysis and network design.
The authors report that extensive experiments across eight benchmarks validate MILI's effectiveness against state-of-the-art baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNNs model molecules as graphs for molecule representation learning.
Molecule representation models face out-of-distribution changes, while invariant learning seeks to reduce prediction variation across environments.
Privileged substructures are described as invariant functional groups that dominate molecular properties, motivating compatible environment splits.
MILI combines a substructure invariance constraint, environment-split criteria, and a dual-head GNN.
The authors report mutual enhancement from the unified design and effectiveness across eight benchmarks.

source_observation.claim: The abstract identifies privileged substructures as invariant functional groups that dominate molecular properties across distribution shifts.

interpretation.claim: Domain-specific structures that remain stable under shift may provide a useful basis for invariant representation learning.

application.claim: When designing invariant models, identify stable domain structures and use them to constrain representations or define environments.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that privileged substructures are invariant or dominant for domains beyond the described molecule setting.

unknowns: The eight benchmark identities, evaluation metrics, quantitative results, and variance estimates are unspecified.
The environment-split criteria are not stated in detail.
Theoretical assumptions and proof details are omitted.
Implementation details and computational costs are omitted.
